---
title: "Scatterplots"
---

Scatterplots are one of the most fundamental tools for visualizing the relationship between two continuous variables (or
variables that we wish to treat as continuous). Each point on the plot represents one observational unit's values on the
two plotted variables. This makes scatterplots particularly useful for identifying trends, clusters, and extreme values
in the data.

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
#| context: setup

download.file("https://openstatprog.com/raw-data/diabetes.rds", "diabetes.rds")
diabetes <- readRDS("diabetes.rds")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, include = FALSE}
diabetes <- readRDS(here::here("data", "diabetes.rds"))
```

**Do:** We make a simple scatterplot with the `plot()` function. For example, the following code uses the `diabetes` dataset to
visualize the bivariate association between Body Mass Index, `bmi`, and Total Cholesterol, `tc`. Higher body fat is
generally linked to less favorable cholesterol levels in the clinical literature. 

```{r}
plot(y = diabetes$tc, x = diabetes$bmi)
```

**See:** every point represents a different patient's value of BMI and their level of total cholesterol. The points form a cloud with a slight upward trend, suggesting that higher BMI values tend to be associated with higher cholesterol levels, although the variability is substantial.

We can improve the readability by adding axis labels, a title, and adjusting the axis limits. To do so we adjust the
following parameters.

- `ylab`, `xlab`: Define new axis labels
- `main`: Add a plot title
- `ylim`, `xlim`: Define the ranges of the y-axis and x-axis

**Predict:** these arguments only change the plot's cosmetics; before running the code, predict whether the underlying
pattern of points (their positions relative to each other) will change at all.

```{r}
plot(y = diabetes$tc,
     x = diabetes$bmi,
     ylab = "Total Cholesterol",
     xlab = "Body Mass Index",
     main = "Relation between BMI and Cholesterol",
     ylim = c(0, 350),
     xlim = c(0, 50))
```

**Explain:** as predicted, the points themselves sit in exactly the same relative positions as before; only the labels,
title, and the visible range of each axis have changed, making the figure easier to read without altering the
underlying data.

When we apply `plot()` to a data frame containing only numeric columns, we generate a scatterplot matrix: a grid of
scatterplots showing all the pairwise relationships. **Do:** Run the code below that selects 5 numeric columns.

```{r}
plot(diabetes[c("age", "bmi", "tc", "glu", "progress")])
```

**See:** The grid contains 5 &times; 5 = 25 panels, one for every pair of the 5 selected variables
(including each variable plotted against itself along the diagonal). Reading across a row or down a column lets us
compare one variable's relationship with every other variable at a glance, without having to build each scatterplot
individually.

::: practice

## Practice Exercise
Using the diabetes dataset, make a scatterplot of total cholesterol on the y-axis against age on the x-axis. Add meaningful axis labels and a title.

- The `diabetes` dataset is already loaded in the working directory of this *webr* session.

## {{< var tab_title.solution >}}

```{r}
     x = diabetes$age,
     ylab = "Total Cholesterol",
     xlab = "Age",
     main = "Relation between Age and Cholesterol")
```
